Let's go with one class per cpp/hpp file.
What you've asked for isn't something we enforce today.  I'm not going to start enforcing it on this commit.

Do you have any opinion on the matter? I think it's quite convenient to have one file per class and also helps to quickly find the relevant files.

It can also help to avoid git conflicts and does not require us to make a choice as to the order of the classes inside the file.

It also helps to avoid including more than what is necessary.

> Do you have any opinion on the matter?

My opinion is that:
1. It doesn't matter in an engineering sense.
2. Trying to enforce the above isn't worth the effort
3. Discussing general c++ "rules" like this in a single review isn't the right place for that discussion.
4. When and when not to use compile units is subtle and has unintended impacts (binary size being one common one).

Most importantly, I don't want to be gating inclusion of working code on arbitrary coding guidelines.  I want the rules we enforce to have an impact on maintainability or engineering.  Keep in mind, I didn't write this app;  It was an app written by someone at Google that decided that getting it upstream wasn't worth the effort, by in part likely because of rules like the above.  Looking at Googles bmc open source tree and making assumptions from that, it's been in use for years without issues.  It is more important that people feel like they have a path to get code into the build than it is to enforce things like number of and variety of compile units.  I don't know any widely-used standard that enforces c++ to the level of "this should be a header".

And remember, if there's problems that this causes in a practical sense, we can always adapt and refactor (as you do quite often, and I appreciate).

> And remember, if there's problems that this causes in a practical sense, we can always adapt and refactor

There's a lot of code in entity-manager that could not be refactored, either for compatibility reasons or because maintainers were not interested in putting in the work required to review patches.

> When and when not to use compile units is subtle and has unintended impacts (binary size being one common one).

That's something to fix in compiler toolchains, not in our code. It's not our job to do the compiler's job.

If you really care about binary size then you should not compile it as a separate binary but instead make a single binary from it and the other applications in this repo. Similar to how we did it for bmcweb.

That will improve overall binary size consumption in the image, trading binary size for clarity and other things.

> > And remember, if there's problems that this causes in a practical sense, we can always adapt and refactor
> 
> There's a lot of code in entity-manager that could not be refactored, either for compatibility reasons or because maintainers were not interested in putting in the work required to review patches.

We've now pivoted from compile units (which ARE refactorable if needed) to a general discussion about your attempts to enforce PDI on EM.  Happy to discuss with you in the appropriate forum, but lets keep this discussion about this patch.  The original ask was "one class per cpp/hpp", which I don't believe is neccesary.


> 
> > When and when not to use compile units is subtle and has unintended impacts (binary size being one common one).
> 
> That's something to fix in compiler toolchains, not in our code. It's not our job to do the compiler's job.

The above is your opinion and I disagree with it very much, but this is again, not the right forum for making general "not my problem" arguments.

> 
> If you really care about binary size then you should not compile it as a separate binary but instead make a single binary from it and the other applications in this repo. Similar to how we did it for bmcweb.

Everything is about tradeoffs, and for better or worse all the existing detection daemons are currently separate applications.  I'm not going to change that paradigm in this patch, but happy to discuss if you have thoughts there.

> 
> That will improve overall binary size consumption in the image, trading binary size for clarity and other things.

Not a change I'm planning to make in this patch as it would be against the current status quo.  Happy to discuss elsewhere

I believe this discussion has run its course on the original ask which was one cpp/hpp per file.  If we determine this to be the right thing to do later, it is a pretty doable refactor.
These are not templates, why are they in a hpp file?
To reduce the number of compile units.  As written this is only included from one compile unit.

> To reduce the number of compile units. 

meson supports unity builds if you want to reduce the number of build TUs.

As written this is making a tradeoff with incremental compilation performance which is an quite important for contributors using smaller machines.

See https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#sf2-a-header-file-must-not-contain-object-definitions-or-non-inline-function-definitions

I don't think this interface is documented to exist in PDI.


Do you plan to document it there or is there already a change pending to get it added?

> I don't think this interface is documented to exist in PDI.
> 

Nor should it be.

> 
> Do you plan to document it there or is there already a change pending to get it added?

Nope, this is the equivalent of FRUDevice, it's an internal API for EM to use internally, and is not stable for general purpose use.

I still believe it would be good to properly develop and document this interface in the PDI.

The documentation aspect will be quite useful for folks to be able to look up this interface and the meaning of it's properties and the intention behind it.

Are you saying that interfaces only used inside one repository cannot be documented to potentially be re-used elsewhere?

There are a lot of interfaces in the PDI which are only exposed or consumed by a single repo.

> I still believe it would be good to properly develop and document this interface in the PDI.

Feel free.  I question the word "properly".  This repo doesn't use PDI, and hasn't since its creation.  Imposing that on new patches isn't something I'm prepared to do.  You may think PDI is proper, and that's fine, but it's a much longer process than reviewing code, and I personally find that process loses details that are required to make things work.

I fully admit that Patrick and I disagree in this regard, and that too, is fine, we can all still make progress.

> 
> The documentation aspect will be quite useful for folks to be able to look up this interface and the meaning of it's properties and the intention behind it.

PDI is yaml files, to call it documentation is a stretch.  Possibly you prefer that abstraction, which is fine.

> 
> Are you saying that interfaces only used inside one repository cannot be documented to potentially be re-used elsewhere?

For the second time today, that's not what I said and somehow a statement made about one API has been changed to apply to all cases in all scenarios (which is not what I said).  What I said is that THIS interface is not intended to be re-used elsewhere as written.  It's intended to be used for EM probes.  If someone wants to reuse it for non probes, that deserves a discussion, at which point possibly a PDI review is the right approach.

> 
> There are a lot of interfaces in the PDI which are only exposed or consumed by a single repo.

Not saying otherwise.
